title: One Loop Runs the Whole Project: Plan, Measure, Decide, Record
summary: The owner's control system from this phase is one loop, not six topics. A charter sets who decides, the work breakdown ties scope to cost and schedule, and every decision is measured against a baseline and written down. This checkpoint lesson rebuilds that loop so you can run it from memory.
body:
Charter, scope, schedule, cost, procurement and safety are not six subjects. They are one loop: plan the work, measure it against the plan, decide what to do about the gap, and record the decision so the next measurement starts from the truth.

Recall

Q. Name OSHA's Focus Four hazards in construction.

A. Falls, struck-by, caught-in or caught-between, and electrocution. They account for a large share of construction deaths, which is why the United States Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) targets them.

Q. What is a guaranteed maximum price (GMP)?

A. A contract price the construction manager agrees not to exceed for a defined scope, with costs above it carried by the contractor unless the scope changes. Savings below it are shared or returned as the contract says. The split is commercial practice, not a standard.

Q. What is a maturity wall?

A. A cluster of loans falling due at the same time, so that a borrower must refinance a large share of its debt in one market window. If credit tightens in that window, a solvent borrower can still fail.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, an owner who has never run a project usually thinks control means watching the contractor. It does not. Control means you decided in advance what good looks like, you can see within a week when reality departs from it, and someone with the authority to act on the gap actually acts and writes it down. Without all four parts, you are not in control. You are a spectator with a cheque book.

This is a checkpoint week. Each seat revisits the hardest idea of the owner's control phase from its own angle. Today is the frame that holds the other six days together.

Plan: the charter and the baseline

In plain English: before work starts, write down who decides what, and freeze a picture of the plan you will measure against.

The professional framing has two documents. The project charter names the project's purpose, the owner's representative, the approval authorities and the reporting cadence. The baseline is the approved scope, budget and schedule at a fixed date. The work breakdown structure (WBS), a numbered tree that splits the project into deliverables, is the spine that ties them together: each WBS element carries a cost code in the budget and an activity in the schedule. When those three line up, one question, "how is the mechanical package doing?", has one answer in money and one answer in time.

A worked example, hypothetical round numbers. Your charter sets an approval matrix. The owner's representative may approve a change up to 25,000 dollars. Changes from 25,000 to 250,000 dollars need you. Anything above 250,000 dollars, or anything touching structure, life safety or the lender's collateral, needs you and written notice to the lender. In month six the contractor proposes a 180,000 dollar substitution of the window system. Your representative cannot approve it, even though it saves money, because it falls in your band and touches the building envelope. The matrix did its job: it put the decision where the risk sits.

Measure: one set of numbers, three views

In plain English: compare what you planned, what you have earned and what you have spent, every month, on the same cost codes.

Earned value management gives the vocabulary. Planned value is the budgeted cost of work scheduled to date. Earned value is the budgeted cost of work actually completed. Actual cost is what you spent. Two ratios fall out. The cost performance index (CPI) is earned value divided by actual cost; below 1.0 means each dollar spent buys less than a dollar of planned work. The schedule performance index (SPI) is earned value divided by planned value; below 1.0 means you are behind. On Day 3 Nadia turns these into money and return.

A second worked example, hypothetical. At month eight, planned value is 8,000,000 dollars, earned value is 7,200,000 dollars and actual cost is 8,000,000 dollars. CPI is 7.2 divided by 8.0, which is 0.90. SPI is 7.2 divided by 8.0, also 0.90. The project is ten percent behind and ten percent over on what it has done. Neither number tells you why; both tell you where to look this week.

Say that out loud now.

Earned value over actual cost is cost efficiency; earned value over planned value is schedule efficiency; below one on either means look now.

Decide and record: change control and the decision log

Measurement without decision is a report nobody reads. Change control is the procedure that turns a gap or a proposal into a decision: a written request, an impact on cost and time, a recommendation, an approval at the right level, and an update to the baseline. The owner decision log is the record: date, decision, who made it, what it cost, what evidence they saw. Petra's float ownership, Quincy's cost-to-complete and Duke's job hazard analysis all feed this loop; none of them works if decisions are made in corridors and never written.

How the best do it

Disciplined owners on large programmes run a fixed monthly rhythm: the contractor's report lands on a set day, the owner's team reconciles it against its own cost and schedule view within days, and a short decision meeting follows in which every open change is either approved, rejected or given a deadline. Nothing stays open without an owner's name beside it. A small developer can copy the rhythm with one spreadsheet, one fixed meeting day and one rule: every item on the agenda leaves with a decision or a date.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: how a change is coded, to land, building or a deductible expense, can change its tax treatment; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: an approval outside the matrix may bind you anyway if the contractor reasonably relied on it. Banking: lenders read change logs at every draw, and an untidy log costs you credibility. Governance: the approval matrix belongs in a board or partner resolution, not only in a project document. Estate: a project only you can run is a key-person risk; the charter is how someone else could step in. Exit: a buyer's diligence on a finished building reads the decision log to find latent problems.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer on the approval matrix in the contract; cost consultant on the earned value baseline.

The loop in one month

Here is how the loop runs in a single month on a small project, hypothetical. On the fifth working day the contractor's report and payment application arrive. By the eighth, your cost consultant has measured earned value on the same cost codes and your owner's representative has updated the change log. On the tenth, you hold a one-hour decision meeting: safety first, then each variance above a threshold you set, say 2 percent of a cost code, then every open change. Each item leaves with a decision or a date. On the twelfth, you sign the draw certificate, because only now do you know the numbers behind it. On the fifteenth, the decision log and a one-page summary go to your partners and lender. The same calendar repeats every month. The value of the loop is less in any one meeting than in the rhythm: problems surface in weeks, not quarters, and nobody can claim they were not told.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a baseline that quietly moves. If every approved change rewrites the plan without a trace, the project never looks late or over budget, and you discover the truth at the end. The control is a frozen original baseline kept alongside the current one, with every difference explained by a logged change.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the contractor's monthly report as the measurement. It is the contractor's view of the contractor's work. The owner needs an independent view on the same cost codes, even if it is only a simple one.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught the in-balance test: undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the cost to complete. That test is only as honest as the owner's control loop. A cost to complete built from logged changes and earned value is a forecast; one built from budget remaining is a hope. The loop you rebuilt today is what makes the lender's test pass for the right reason.

Recap

Plan with a charter, an approval matrix and a frozen baseline tied together by the work breakdown. Measure monthly with earned value on the same cost codes. Decide through change control at the right authority level, and record every decision in the owner decision log.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: the Sampoong Department Store collapse, and what happens when the owner overrides the people paid to say no.
checklist: I can draw the plan, measure, decide, record loop from memory.
My charter names the owner's representative and the reporting cadence.
I have an approval matrix with money bands and a separate rule for structure and life safety.
Every WBS element has one cost code and one schedule activity.
I calculate CPI and SPI monthly on my own numbers, not only the contractor's.
I keep the original baseline frozen beside the current one.
Every change has a written request, a cost and time impact, and a named approver.
My decision log records the evidence each decision was based on.
head: Field checklist
speak: The owner's control system is one loop: plan, measure, decide, record. Plan means a charter that names who decides, an approval matrix with money bands, and a frozen baseline of scope, cost and schedule, tied together by the work breakdown structure so each element has one cost code and one schedule activity. Measure means earned value every month: earned value over actual cost gives the cost performance index, earned value over planned value gives the schedule performance index, and below one on either means look now. Decide means change control: a written request, its cost and time impact, a recommendation and approval at the right level. Record means the owner decision log: date, decision, who, cost and evidence. The biggest risk is a baseline that quietly moves, so I keep the original frozen beside the current one. The contractor's report is the contractor's view; I keep my own.
terms: Baseline — the approved scope, budget and schedule frozen at a date, against which all progress is measured.
Cost performance index (CPI) — earned value divided by actual cost; below 1.0 means the work done cost more than planned.
Approval matrix — a table that sets who may approve which decisions, by money band and by type of risk.

hostile.q: Your CPI is 0.90 at month eight. Why should I believe the remaining budget holds?
hostile.a: You should not, on that number alone, and I am not asking you to. A CPI of 0.90 means each dollar has bought ninety cents of planned work. If that persists, the estimate at completion rises by roughly a tenth of the remaining budget. I have traced the variance to two cost codes, reforecast both from bought-out subcontracts, and I will show you the revised cost to complete line by line, with the contingency draw it implies and what I am doing to stop the trend.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole (audit and integrity) assisting
title: Sampoong 1995: When the Owner Overrode the People Paid to Say No
summary: The Sampoong Department Store in Seoul collapsed on 29 June 1995 and 502 people died. The building had been changed from its original design during construction, against professional objection, and warning signs on the final day were not acted on. The lesson for an owner is that approval authorities and hold points exist precisely for the day you want to ignore them.
body:
On 29 June 1995 the Sampoong Department Store in Seoul collapsed in the early evening and 502 people died. The engineering failed at the end, but the control system had failed years earlier, when the owner made the people who said no leave the room.

Recall

Q. What is the multi-employer doctrine?

A. An OSHA enforcement policy under which more than one employer on a site can be cited for the same hazard: the employer that created it, exposed workers to it, was responsible for correcting it, or controlled the site. Verify the current policy against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. What is bid levelling?

A. Adjusting competing bids onto the same scope, by adding missing items and removing extras, so that prices can be compared honestly before award.

Q. What is a leverage spiral?

A. A loop in which falling values breach loan covenants, forcing asset sales or cash calls, which push values down further and trigger more breaches.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this is a governance case as much as an engineering one. You will own buildings. Owners do not usually design them or pour the concrete, but owners decide what changes, who approves, and when to stop. The broad facts below are widely reported from the official investigation and the trials that followed. I keep to them, avoid technical figures I cannot confirm, and describe the mechanism rather than every detail.

1. Timeline

The building was planned in the late 1980s in the Seocho district of Seoul and was originally designed for a different use, generally reported as an office building. During construction the owner converted it to a large department store. The original contractor objected to changes it considered unsafe and was replaced; the owner's own construction affiliate finished the job. The store opened at the end of the 1980s with an extra floor added above the original design. In the years that followed, heavy equipment on the roof was relocated. In the months before the collapse, cracks appeared. On the day itself, cracking worsened sharply during the afternoon. Senior management met, and the store was not evacuated. The building collapsed shortly before six in the evening.

2. Key decisions

Four decisions carried the outcome. Changing the use of the building after structural design was complete. Removing or thinning structural elements to open up retail floor and fit escalators. Adding a storey and heavy loads without re-engineering the whole structure. And on the final day, choosing to keep trading rather than empty the building.

3. Assumptions

Behind each decision sat an assumption nobody tested in writing. That a structure designed for one use could carry another. That a contractor who refused a change was being difficult rather than right. That cracks were cosmetic until proven otherwise. And that closing a store for a day was a large cost while the risk of staying open was small. Every one of those assumptions inverted the true balance of risk.

4. Incentives

Retail floor area earns money; columns and thicker slabs do not. Every change that added sellable space or reduced construction cost improved the owner's return on paper. A contractor that refused cost the owner time. On the last day, an evacuation meant lost sales and public embarrassment. The incentives all pointed the same way, which is exactly when an owner needs an independent person with the authority to point the other way.

Say that out loud now.

When every incentive points one way, the control has to point the other.

5. Warning signs ignored

The contractor's refusal was the first and loudest signal: a professional with money at stake chose to lose the job rather than do the work. The cracks were the second. Reports of noise and vibration from relocated roof equipment were a third. On the final afternoon the signs were visible to staff. Each warning was treated as a problem to manage rather than evidence to act on.

6. Point of no return

Engineers will tell you the structure was compromised long before the day, so in one sense the point of no return was the decision to cut structure and add load without full redesign. For the people inside, the point of no return was the afternoon meeting that did not order an evacuation. Until that meeting, every life could still have been saved by walking out of the door.

7. Root cause

Cole's finding, stated as an auditor would: the owner held design authority, construction authority and operating authority in one hand, and there was no independent person whose written approval was required before structure, use or load changed. When the original contractor exercised a de facto veto, it was removed. Courts later convicted the chairman and others, and public officials were also convicted in connection with the approvals; the exact charges and sentences are on the court record and should be checked there. The technical failure was in slabs and columns. The root cause was a control system with no brakes.

The owner's translation

A worked example on your own scale, hypothetical. You own a four-storey building under construction. A tenant wants a heavy rooftop unit, and your contractor says the roof framing "should be fine". Your approval matrix routes any change to structure or load to the engineer of record, whatever the price. The engineer asks for the unit's operating weight and the support layout, checks the framing, and specifies two added beams at a cost of 40,000 dollars. You approve it in the log with the engineer's letter attached. The cost is small. The record is the proof that you did not decide alone.

A second example. On a Saturday your superintendent reports new diagonal cracking at a transfer beam. The rule is evacuate, then convene: clear the area, call the engineer of record, and discuss cost only after people are safe. Decide that rule now, in writing, while nothing is cracking.

Cole's audit questions for any change

Cole's note. When I audit a project, I pick changes at random and ask the same questions of each, because the questions reveal whether a control exists or only a procedure. Who requested the change, and in writing? Who approved it, and did they hold that authority under the approval matrix on that date? Was the engineer of record asked, and is the answer a signed letter or a remembered phone call? What load, use or code assumption did the change alter, and was the calculation updated? Was there a hold point before the work was covered up, and who released it? Where is the change in the decision log, and does the cost in the log match the cost paid? If any answer is "I would have to ask", the control is not working. On a well-run project, every answer is a document that can be produced within an hour. On the projects that fail, the answers live in people's heads, and the people who held the inconvenient answers have often already left.

Run those questions on your own projects before anyone else does. They take an afternoon and they are the cheapest insurance you will ever buy.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk for an owner is holding every authority at once and treating professional objection as friction. The control is a required independent sign-off, by the engineer of record, on any change to structure, use or load, logged before work proceeds.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner replaces the adviser who says no with one who says yes, and feels decisive. Replacing an objector is the moment to get a second, independent opinion, not to stop asking.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and ask why. Run one on any change to structure or use, and the Sampoong story writes itself. In Week 49, Marco and Quincy built change control; this case is what change control is for.

Recap

A change of use, structural cuts and added load, made over professional objection, left a building that could not stand. Warnings were managed rather than acted on, and the final afternoon meeting kept people inside. Rule 54: no change to structure, use or load proceeds without the engineer of record's written approval in the change log, and a structural warning means evacuate first and meet second.

Next: Nadia, on The Money: what weak control costs, in earned value, cost to complete and return.
checklist: My approval matrix routes every change to structure, use or load to the engineer of record, at any price.
I have written down that a structural warning means evacuate first and meet second.
When an adviser refuses a change, I get a second independent opinion before replacing them.
My change log attaches the engineer's letter to every structural approval.
I know who on site has authority to stop work and clear an area.
I keep design, construction and operating authority from sitting with one person unchecked.
I treat cracks, vibration and unusual noise as evidence to act on, not problems to manage.
head: Field checklist
speak: The Sampoong Department Store in Seoul collapsed on 29 June 1995 and 502 people died. During construction the owner converted a building designed for another use into a department store, thinned or removed structure to open floors, and added a storey and heavy loads. The original contractor objected and was replaced. Cracks appeared in the months before the collapse, and on the final afternoon management met and did not evacuate. The technical failure was in slabs and columns, but the root cause was governance: the owner held design, construction and operating authority together, and no independent person had to approve changes to structure, use or load. My rule is Rule 54: no change to structure, use or load goes ahead without the engineer of record's written approval in the change log, and any structural warning means evacuate first and meet second.
terms: Change of use — altering what a building is used for, which can change the loads, occupancy and code requirements it must meet.
Engineer of record — the licensed engineer responsible for the structural design, whose approval a structural change requires.
De facto veto — the practical power to stop a decision by refusing to carry it out, even without formal authority.

hostile.q: Your tenant wants a heavier rooftop unit and your contractor says the roof is fine. Why are you spending 40,000 dollars on an engineer's check and new beams?
hostile.a: Because the contractor's opinion is not an approval, and my rule is that any change to structure, use or load goes to the engineer of record at any price. The engineer checked the unit's operating weight against the framing and specified two beams. The 40,000 dollars is logged with the engineer's letter. If I skipped it and the roof deflected, the cost would be a repair, a claim and a building nobody trusts.

rule: Rule 54: No change to a building's structure, use or loads goes ahead without the engineer of record's written approval recorded in the change log, whatever it costs or saves, and any structural warning means evacuate first and meet second.

title: What Weak Control Costs: From an Index Below One to a Lower Return
summary: A cost performance index below one is not an abstract score; it compounds into a higher estimate at completion, a larger draw on contingency, more interest and a lower return. This lesson turns the owner's control metrics into money and shows where the damage lands on profit and on your own balance sheet.
body:
An index below one is money already lost and money about to be lost. Convert it into an estimate at completion, then into contingency, interest and profit, and you will know whether a project is wobbling or failing.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 54?

A. No change to structure, use or loads goes ahead without the engineer of record's written approval in the change log, and a structural warning means evacuate first and meet second.

Q. What does buyout mean in procurement?

A. Awarding the subcontracts and purchase orders after the main contract is signed, which turns allowances and estimates into committed prices and reveals savings or overruns against the budget.

Q. What is a guarantee call?

A. A lender's demand that a guarantor pay under a guarantee, for example to fund a cost overrun or complete the project, after the trigger in the guarantee has occurred.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a contractor can tell you a project is "a little behind and a little over" for months. Each month that sounds survivable. The numbers say otherwise, and they say it early. The owner who converts the indices into dollars in month four makes decisions; the owner who waits for month fourteen makes deposits.

From index to estimate at completion

In plain English: if the work keeps costing what it has cost so far, how much will the whole project cost?

The professional framing is the estimate at completion (EAC). The simplest version divides the budget at completion by the cost performance index. A version that is often more realistic for a project running late as well as over divides the remaining budget by the product of the two indices, because late work usually costs more, not less. Neither formula is a forecast you should sign. They are alarms that tell you how big the bottom-up reforecast is likely to be.

A worked example, hypothetical round numbers. Hard cost budget at completion is 20,000,000 dollars. At month eight, earned value is 7,200,000 dollars, actual cost 8,000,000 dollars and planned value 8,000,000 dollars, so CPI and SPI are both 0.90. Simple EAC is 20,000,000 divided by 0.90, about 22,200,000 dollars. The pessimistic version: remaining budget is 20,000,000 less 7,200,000, which is 12,800,000 dollars. Divided by 0.90 times 0.90, which is 0.81, that gives about 15,800,000 dollars. Add the 8,000,000 already spent and the estimate at completion is about 23,800,000 dollars. So the honest range is roughly 22,200,000 to 23,800,000 dollars against a 20,000,000 dollar budget.

Say that out loud now.

Budget divided by CPI is the optimistic alarm; remaining budget divided by CPI times SPI is the pessimistic one.

Where the overrun lands

An overrun is paid in a fixed order. First by hard-cost contingency, then by any owner's contingency, then by equity, and if the loan is out of balance, by a deposit before the next draw. Suppose your contingency is 1,000,000 dollars. On the optimistic alarm you need 2,200,000 dollars, so contingency is gone and 1,200,000 dollars must come from somewhere. Delay adds interest. On a hypothetical loan averaging 12,000,000 dollars drawn at 8 percent a year, each extra month costs about 80,000 dollars. An SPI of 0.90 on a 20-month build suggests about two extra months, roughly 160,000 dollars.

Now the profit. Suppose the finished building is worth 32,000,000 dollars and the total cost was planned at 28,000,000 dollars, a planned profit of 4,000,000 dollars. Add 1,200,000 dollars of uncovered overrun and 160,000 dollars of interest and profit falls to about 2,640,000 dollars, a drop of about a third. On the pessimistic alarm the extra cost is roughly 2,800,000 dollars beyond contingency, and profit falls to about 1,000,000 dollars. A ten percent slip in two indices has cut profit by a third to three quarters. That is leverage working against you: the overrun is a small share of cost but a large share of profit.

The return the investor sees

Your equity partner does not see CPI. The partner sees return. If equity was 8,000,000 dollars expecting 4,000,000 dollars of profit, the equity multiple was planned at 1.5 times. At 2,640,000 dollars of profit and the same equity, it falls to about 1.33 times. If you must put in 1,200,000 dollars more equity to cover the gap, the multiple on 9,200,000 dollars of equity is about 1.29 times, and the return arrives two months later, which pushes the internal rate of return down further. Report the indices to yourself; report the multiple and its range to your partner, early.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note. Your personal balance sheet carries this project twice: as equity at risk and, if you signed a cost-overrun guarantee, as a contingent liability. When the pessimistic alarm rings, mark your own liquidity floor against the uncovered overrun. If the floor cannot absorb it without selling something you need, you have learned your guarantee is larger than your reserve. This is conceptual; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The efficiency the rest of the job needs

One more number turns the alarm into a test of the contractor's promise. Ask what efficiency the remaining work must achieve to finish on budget. Divide the work still to earn by the money still available. On the same example, the work still to earn is 20,000,000 less 7,200,000, which is 12,800,000 dollars. The money left in the budget is 20,000,000 less 8,000,000, which is 12,000,000 dollars. 12.8 divided by 12.0 is about 1.07. So to land on budget, every dollar spent from now on must buy about 1.07 dollars of planned work, when every dollar so far has bought 90 cents.

That is the honest reply to "we'll recover". Recovery from 0.90 to 1.07 for the rest of the job is a swing of about a fifth in productivity. It happens occasionally, usually when an early problem was isolated and has been fixed. It almost never happens on a trend. When the required efficiency is well above anything the job has achieved, stop planning for recovery and start funding the gap.

A second check, on the monthly index. Suppose the cumulative CPI moved from 0.88 to 0.90 this month. That sounds like improvement. But if this month alone earned 900,000 dollars of work for 950,000 dollars of cost, the monthly index is about 0.95: better than the average, still below one. The trend is improving and still losing money. Report both numbers; never report only the one that sounds better.

A contingency report that tells the truth

A worked example of the report, hypothetical. Contingency was 1,000,000 dollars. To date, 350,000 dollars has been drawn for genuine unknowns: rock in one footing and a utility relocation the survey could not show. Another 250,000 dollars has been drawn to cover two cost codes running at an index of about 0.85. The first number is contingency doing its job. The second is contingency hiding a trend, and it will keep growing every month the trend continues. Report them on separate lines, with the percentage of the project complete beside the percentage of contingency spent. If 60 percent of contingency is gone at 45 percent complete, and most of the riskiest work is still ahead, the report should say so in its first sentence, not its last.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating contingency as the plan for overruns rather than as the plan for the unknown. Once contingency is absorbing a trend, the next surprise lands on equity. The control is a monthly contingency report that separates draws for genuine unknowns from draws that fund a performance trend.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner averages the indices away: "CPI was 0.88 last month and 0.92 this month, so we are improving." Cumulative indices move slowly and hide trends. Read the cumulative index for the size of the problem and the monthly index for its direction.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage taught the equity multiple and warned that IRR rewards speed. An overrun that also delays the project is hit twice: once on profit and once on time. That is why the pessimistic alarm uses both indices.

Recap

Convert indices into an estimate at completion with an optimistic and a pessimistic alarm. Pay the overrun in order: contingency, equity, deposit. Price the delay as interest. Translate the result into the investor's multiple, and mark your own liquidity against any guarantee.

Next: LEX, on The Rules: the paper behind owner control, from approval authority to notice clauses and the multi-employer doctrine.
checklist: I calculate both the optimistic and the pessimistic estimate at completion every month.
I compare the alarm range with a bottom-up reforecast before reporting.
I know the order in which an overrun is paid: contingency, equity, deposit.
I price delay as monthly interest on the average drawn balance.
I report the equity multiple range to my partners as soon as an index falls below one.
My contingency report separates unknowns from performance trends.
I have marked my liquidity floor against any cost-overrun guarantee.
head: Field checklist
speak: An index below one is money. If the cost performance index is 0.90 on a 20 million dollar budget, the simple estimate at completion is budget divided by CPI, about 22.2 million. The pessimistic version divides the remaining budget by CPI times SPI, which gives about 23.8 million when both indices are 0.90. That range is an alarm, not a forecast; I follow it with a bottom-up reforecast. The overrun is paid in order: contingency, then equity, then a deposit if the loan falls out of balance. Delay adds interest, about 80 thousand dollars a month on 12 million drawn at 8 percent. On a planned 4 million profit, a ten percent slip in both indices can cut profit by a third to three quarters, and the equity multiple falls from 1.5 to around 1.3. I report the range early, and I mark my personal liquidity against any guarantee.
terms: Estimate at completion (EAC) — the forecast total cost of the project given performance so far.
Budget at completion — the total approved budget for the work, used as the base for earned value calculations.
Contingent liability — an obligation that becomes real only if an event occurs, such as a guarantee being called.

hostile.q: Your contractor says the 0.90 CPI will recover. Why are you already telling investors about a lower multiple?
hostile.a: Because cumulative indices rarely recover on their own, and investors judge me on whether I told them early. I am reporting a range, not a loss: the optimistic alarm, the pessimistic alarm, and my bottom-up reforecast between them, with the actions under way on the two cost codes driving it. If performance improves, the range narrows and they hear good news. If it does not, they were warned in month eight, not month eighteen.

title: The Paper Behind Control: Authority, Notice, Price and Shared Safety Duties
summary: Owner control rests on documents that decide who can bind the project, how changes and claims must be notified, what a guaranteed maximum price really guarantees, and how safety duties are shared on a multi-employer site. This lesson revisits those rules as concepts, so you know what to ask your lawyer and where projects quietly lose their rights.
body:
Control on site is only as strong as the paper behind it. Four sets of rules decide most outcomes: who may bind the project, how notice must be given, what a price actually promises, and who answers for a hazard on a shared site.

Recall

Q. What is the pessimistic estimate at completion?

A. Actual cost to date plus the remaining budget divided by the cost performance index times the schedule performance index. It assumes late work also costs more.

Q. What is the difference between construction management at risk and construction management as agency?

A. At risk, the construction manager holds the trade contracts and usually commits to a price such as a GMP. As agency, it advises the owner, who holds the trade contracts and carries the cost risk.

Q. What is a refinancing gap?

A. The shortfall between a maturing loan and the amount a new lender will advance at that date, which the borrower must fund from equity or another source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most construction disputes are not won on who was morally right. They are won on who gave notice on time, who had authority to agree, and what the contract said the price covered. These are concepts, not a jurisdiction's rules. The exact law depends on where the building sits and which contract form you use; verify each point against the primary source before you rely on it, and have a construction lawyer read your contract before you sign it.

Authority: who can bind the project

In plain English: a promise binds you if someone you allowed to look like your agent made it.

The professional framing is agency. Actual authority is what you gave someone in writing or by instruction. Apparent authority is what a reasonable contractor would believe from how you behaved, for example letting your site representative sign change orders for months without objection. Many legal systems will hold an owner to a change approved under apparent authority, even if your internal approval matrix said otherwise. So the matrix must be in the contract, notified to the contractor, and enforced from the first day.

A worked example, hypothetical. Your contract names your representative and says changes above 25,000 dollars need your signature. For three months you let the representative approve 60,000 dollar changes and you pay them. In month four the representative approves a 200,000 dollar change you dislike. The contractor will argue your conduct widened the representative's authority. Your best defence was never paying the earlier ones without your own signature.

Notice: rights that expire

Most construction contracts require a party to give written notice of a claimed change, delay or claim within a set period, sent in a set form to a set address. Some make notice a condition precedent: miss it and the right to more time or money is lost. A clause that cuts off a claim after a period is called a time bar. Courts in different places treat time bars differently, from strict enforcement to relief where the other side knew anyway; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

For an owner the rule cuts both ways. Your contractor must give you notice, and your own lender, insurer and consultants often require notice from you. A delayed notice to your builder's risk insurer can cost you cover. Build a notice register: every clause that requires notice, its period, its form and its address.

Say that out loud now.

No notice, no claim: every right with a time limit goes in my notice register on day one.

Price: what a GMP promises

A guaranteed maximum price guarantees a ceiling on the contractor's reimbursable cost for a defined scope. It does not guarantee your total project cost. Owner changes, unforeseen conditions the contract allocates to you, allowances that run over, escalation clauses and excluded work all sit outside it. The exclusions and qualifications list is where the real price lives.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A GMP is 18,000,000 dollars, including a 600,000 dollar allowance for curtain wall anchors and a qualification that steel is priced at a stated index level with adjustment above a band. The anchors cost 900,000 dollars and steel rises past the band, adding 350,000 dollars. Your "guaranteed" price is now 18,650,000 dollars before a single owner change, and both increases are contractually correct. You did not lose a dispute. You misread the guarantee.

Safety: duties shared across employers

On an American site, OSHA's construction standards in 29 CFR Part 1926 set the rules, and its multi-employer citation policy lets more than one employer be cited for one hazard: the one that created it, the one whose workers were exposed, the one responsible for correcting it, and the one that controlled the site. An owner who directs the work closely can drift toward the controlling role. Courts and agencies weigh the facts; verify the current policy and case law against the primary source before you rely on it. The practical rule is to control safety through the contract, by requiring a site-specific safety plan, prequalification and reporting, rather than by directing trades yourself.

A change order is a small contract

Every signed change order is a contract amendment, and the words at the bottom matter more than the price at the top. Many change order forms say the agreed adjustment is a full and final settlement of all cost and time arising from the change, including knock-on delay. Others let the contractor reserve its rights to claim time or disruption later. Those two forms produce very different exposure from the same price.

A worked example, hypothetical. You agree a 120,000 dollar change to move a stair. The contractor signs a form that reserves its rights on time. Four months later it claims 300,000 dollars of disruption, saying the stair change pushed the core and the trades behind it. Had the form required a full and final settlement, including time, the contractor would have had to price that risk before signing, and you could have decided whether the stair was worth 420,000 dollars. Neither form is wrong. The owner's mistake is not reading which one was signed.

The practical controls are simple. Use one change order form, approved by your lawyer, for every change. Require each change order to state its time impact in days, even if the answer is zero. Refuse open-ended reservations of rights unless you have agreed them deliberately, and record each one in the decision log. And never let work proceed on a verbal instruction "to be papered later": in many systems the paper that arrives later is the contractor's version of what you agreed.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is behaviour that rewrites the contract: paying unauthorised changes, accepting late notices informally, directing trades on site. Each one teaches the other side, and later a tribunal, that the written rules do not mean what they say. The control is consistency: enforce the paper the same way every month, and record every exception in writing as an exception.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner signs a GMP contract believing the project cost is fixed, then skips the exclusions and allowance schedules. Read the qualifications first; they are the price.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught conditions and the difference between a term that binds and one that only describes. A notice clause drafted as a condition precedent is that idea in its hardest form: the condition decides whether the right exists at all.

Recap

Authority comes from paper and from conduct, so enforce the approval matrix from day one. Notice clauses can extinguish rights, so keep a notice register. A GMP caps a defined scope, not your project. Shared safety duties follow control, so manage safety through the contract.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer licensed where the project sits.

Next: Quincy, on The Numbers: reverse engineering a finished overrun back to the control that failed.
checklist: My approval matrix is written into the contract and notified to the contractor.
I never pay a change that lacks the signature the matrix requires.
I keep a notice register with every period, form and address.
I know which notice clauses are conditions precedent.
I have read the GMP exclusions, allowances and escalation qualifications line by line.
I manage safety through contract requirements, not by directing trades myself.
Every exception to the contract is recorded in writing as an exception.
head: Field checklist
speak: Owner control rests on four sets of rules. Authority: a promise binds me if someone I allowed to look like my agent made it, so my approval matrix must be in the contract and enforced from day one; paying unauthorised changes can widen apparent authority. Notice: many contracts require written notice of a change, delay or claim within a set time, and some make it a condition precedent, so missing it loses the right; I keep a notice register for my contractor, my lender and my insurer. Price: a guaranteed maximum price caps the contractor's cost for a defined scope, not my project cost; allowances, escalation and exclusions sit outside it. Safety: on an American site, more than one employer can be cited for one hazard, and an owner who directs trades drifts toward the controlling role, so I manage safety through the contract. A construction lawyer reads every contract before I sign.
terms: Apparent authority — the authority a third party reasonably believes an agent has, based on how the principal behaved.
Time bar — a contract clause that extinguishes a claim if notice is not given within a set period.
Allowance — a sum in the contract price for work not yet fully defined, adjusted to actual cost when the work is priced.

hostile.q: Your GMP is 18 million. Why is your budget carrying more than that for the same scope?
hostile.a: Because the GMP caps the contractor's reimbursable cost for the defined scope, not my project cost. It carries allowances and an escalation qualification, and it excludes some work. I have priced each allowance against current quotes, modelled the escalation band, and listed the exclusions I will buy separately. The gap between the GMP and my budget is that list, line by line, and I can show you each one.

title: Reverse Engineering an Overrun: From the Final Account Back to the Failed Control
summary: This lesson starts at the end: a finished project that cost 2,400,000 dollars more than budget. Working backward through the final account, the change log, escalation, scope gaps and productivity, it assigns every dollar to a cause and then to the control that should have caught it.
body:
An overrun is never one number. Work backward from the final account, split it into causes, and put a name beside each: the control that should have caught it and the month it should have spoken.

Recall

Q. What does a GMP guarantee, and what does it not?

A. It caps the contractor's reimbursable cost for a defined scope. It does not cap owner changes, allowances that run over, escalation outside agreed bands, excluded work or risks the contract leaves with the owner.

Q. What is a schedule of values?

A. The contractor's breakdown of the contract price into line items, used to measure progress and approve payment applications.

Q. Why can a solvent borrower still fail at a maturity wall?

A. Because the loans must be refinanced in one market window, and if credit tightens then, no new lender may advance enough to repay them.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even-numbered week, so we reverse engineer. Every finished project gives you a free lesson if you take it apart. Owners who do this build better budgets on the next job. Owners who do not repeat the same overrun with a new contractor and blame the contractor again.

The finished outcome

Hypothetical round numbers. A building had a hard cost budget of 20,000,000 dollars including 1,000,000 dollars of contingency, so 19,000,000 dollars of priced work. The final account, the agreed total of everything paid to the contractor, is 22,400,000 dollars. The overrun against budget is 2,400,000 dollars. Against priced work it is 3,400,000 dollars, because contingency was fully consumed. That second number is the one to explain.

Step 1: separate owner changes from everything else

Pull every approved change order from the change log and tag each one by who caused it. Owner-directed changes, such as an upgraded lobby and a tenant's request, total 900,000 dollars. These are choices, not failures, provided they were approved at the right level with a cost and time impact. Remaining unexplained: 3,400,000 less 900,000, which is 2,500,000 dollars.

Step 2: allowances and escalation

Compare every allowance with its final cost. Three allowances ran over by a combined 600,000 dollars. An escalation clause on structural steel and copper added 400,000 dollars. Together, 1,000,000 dollars. Remaining: 1,500,000 dollars. The control that should have caught the allowances is buyout tracking: once the trade was bought, the allowance variance was known, often in month three or four.

Step 3: scope gaps

Scope gaps are work nobody priced because it fell between packages, such as firestopping assigned to no trade or temporary protection missing from every bid. Listing changes coded "missing scope" finds 700,000 dollars. Remaining: 800,000 dollars. The control was bid levelling and a scope matrix at procurement: one row per scope item, one column per package, one tick only.

Say that out loud now.

Owner changes, allowances and escalation, scope gaps, then whatever is left is productivity and delay.

Step 4: productivity and delay

The last 800,000 dollars sits in the contractor's general conditions and in trades paid on time-and-materials terms during a three-month delay. General conditions are the contractor's time-related costs, such as site management, cranes and temporary facilities. Suppose they run at 150,000 dollars a month. Three months is 450,000 dollars. The remaining 350,000 dollars is lost productivity on two trades, visible in the monthly cost performance index of those cost codes. The control was earned value by cost code and a look-ahead schedule that showed the slip in time to act.

Step 5: the interest the account does not show

The final account is only hard cost. Three months of delay also cost interest. On a hypothetical average drawn balance of 14,000,000 dollars at 8 percent a year, three months is 14,000,000 times 0.08 times 3 divided by 12, which is 280,000 dollars. Add soft-cost extensions, such as the design team's and the lender's monitor's extra months, of say 120,000 dollars. The true project overrun is 2,400,000 plus 280,000 plus 120,000, about 2,800,000 dollars.

The reconciliation table

CauseDollarsControl that should have spoken
Owner changes900,000Approval matrix and change log
Allowances and escalation1,000,000Buyout tracking
Scope gaps700,000Scope matrix and bid levelling
Delay and productivity800,000Earned value by cost code and look-ahead schedule
Total against priced work3,400,000Less 1,000,000 contingency gives 2,400,000 over budget

A second worked example, a quick check on the same method. If owner changes had been 2,000,000 dollars and scope gaps zero, the same 3,400,000 dollar total would mean the project was well controlled and the owner simply bought more building. Same headline, opposite verdict. That is why the headline alone tells you nothing.

Step 6: turn the table into the next budget

The reconciliation is only worth doing if it changes the next estimate. Take each line and ask what it would have cost to prevent. Scope gaps were 700,000 dollars, or 3.7 percent of the 19,000,000 dollars of priced work. A scope matrix and a day of bid levelling per package cost perhaps 20,000 dollars of consultant time. That is the easiest saving on the table. Allowances overran by 600,000 dollars against, say, 3,000,000 dollars of allowances, a 20 percent overrun. On the next project, either carry allowances at a more realistic level or move them out of the contract and price them yourself before signing.

Escalation of 400,000 dollars was the market, not a failure, but it tells you something about structure: if your contract carries escalation bands, your contingency must carry the risk of crossing them. Delay of 800,000 dollars in the account, plus 400,000 dollars of interest and soft costs outside it, says that time on this project cost roughly 400,000 dollars a month in total. Write that number on the first page of the next schedule review, because it converts every week of float into money.

A second worked example, on contingency. If the next project is similar, a 1,000,000 dollar contingency on 19,000,000 dollars of priced work, about 5 percent, was clearly thin for this delivery method and this level of design. You might raise it, or you might keep it at 5 percent and fix the scope matrix and allowances that consumed it. The second choice is cheaper and more honest. Contingency should pay for what you could not know, not for what you chose not to check.

Who sees the reconciliation

Share the finished table with three audiences, each for a different reason. Your lender sees that you can explain your own overrun, which is the single best predictor of whether it will lend to you again. Your equity partners see which part of the overrun bought them more building and which part was lost, which keeps the conversation about decisions rather than blame. Your next contractor sees, in the bid documents, the scope matrix and allowance discipline you now require, which tells them before they price that the owner checks. Keep the table in your decision journal too. Three projects from now, the pattern across tables will tell you more about your own blind spots than any single job can.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a change log that does not tag the cause, so the reverse engineering becomes an argument rather than an analysis. The control is a cause code on every change at the moment it is raised: owner, design error or omission, unforeseen condition, scope gap, allowance, escalation.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner explains the overrun with the last thing that went wrong, usually the delay, because it was the most recent and the most painful. Delay explained a third of this overrun. Reconcile every dollar before choosing the story.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage taught estimate classes: early estimates deserve wider ranges. Step 3 shows where the width goes: unpriced scope. A contingency sized to a class of estimate is a defence against gaps you have not found yet, not a fund for gaps you could have found by levelling bids.

Recap

Start from the final account, subtract contingency, and split the remainder into owner changes, allowances and escalation, scope gaps, and delay and productivity. Add the interest and soft costs the account hides. Beside each cause, name the control that should have caught it. Change the control on the next project, not just the contractor.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor or cost consultant on the final account.

Next: Marco, in The Room: a full mock monthly project review with the contractor, the lender's monitor and the safety lead.
checklist: I reconcile the final account against priced work, not only against budget.
Every change carries a cause code from the day it is raised.
I track each allowance against buyout and know its variance by month four.
I use a scope matrix with one tick per scope item at procurement.
I know the contractor's general conditions cost per month.
I add interest and soft-cost extensions to any hard-cost overrun.
I change controls after an overrun, not just contractors.
head: Field checklist
speak: An overrun is never one number. On a hypothetical project with a 20 million dollar budget including 1 million of contingency, the final account came in at 22.4 million: 3.4 million over the priced work. Working backward, owner changes explained 900 thousand, allowances and escalation 1 million, scope gaps 700 thousand, and delay and lost productivity 800 thousand. The account hides more: three months of interest on 14 million at 8 percent is 280 thousand, plus soft-cost extensions, so the true overrun was about 2.8 million. Beside each cause I name the control that should have spoken: the change log, buyout tracking, a scope matrix and earned value by cost code. The same headline could mean a badly run job or an owner who simply bought more building, which is why I reconcile every dollar before I choose the story, and why every change carries a cause code from the day it is raised.
terms: Final account — the agreed total of everything paid to the contractor at the end of the contract.
Scope gap — work required to finish the building that no contract package priced or included.
General conditions — the contractor's time-related costs, such as site management, equipment and temporary facilities.

hostile.q: You are over budget by 2.4 million. Why should I lend to you on the next project?
hostile.a: Because I can show you where every dollar went and what I changed. Of 3.4 million over priced work, 900 thousand was my own approved changes, 1 million was allowances and escalation, 700 thousand was scope gaps and 800 thousand was delay. On the next project, every change carries a cause code, allowances are tracked against buyout from month one, procurement uses a scope matrix, and I run earned value by cost code. The controls changed, not just the contractor.

title: Mock Meeting: The Monthly Project Review When Everything Moves at Once
summary: This is the phase's full mock meeting: a monthly project review in which the schedule has slipped, contingency is burning, the lender's monitor is sceptical and the safety lead reports a near miss. It gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind each question, and how to run the room so it leaves with decisions.
body:
The monthly review is where the owner's control system either works or performs. Run it so the room leaves with decisions, owners and dates, and put safety first on the agenda, every time, even when the money is on fire.

Recall

Q. In what order is a cost overrun usually paid?

A. First from contingency, then from equity, and if the loan falls out of balance, by a deposit before the next draw.

Q. What is a look-ahead schedule?

A. A short-range schedule, often three to six weeks, that breaks upcoming activities into detail so constraints can be cleared before the work is due.

Q. What does a lender read in a change log?

A. Whether changes are approved at the right authority, priced with cost and time impact, and whether the pattern suggests a project losing control.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will chair this meeting dozens of times on every project. People will read your state before they read your numbers. If you are anxious, the contractor pads and the monitor digs. If you are calm and specific, the meeting becomes work rather than theatre.

The setup

This is a composite scene with hypothetical numbers. Month nine of an 18-month build. Around the table: the contractor's project manager, the lender's monitor, your cost consultant, the contractor's safety lead and your owner's representative. The facts: SPI 0.88, CPI 0.93, contingency 60 percent spent at 45 percent complete, and on Tuesday a worker's harness arrested a fall from a slab edge where the guardrail had been removed for a delivery and not replaced.

The opening

Say: "Safety first. Tuesday's near miss: what happened, what has changed, and how do we know it is fixed across the site, not just at that edge? Then three decisions today: the recovery plan for the core walls, the two allowances that are running over, and the contingency forecast I will give the lender."

Why that order: safety first is not ceremony. It tells everyone that a guardrail outranks a schedule, and that a fall hazard is one of OSHA's Focus Four, the hazards that kill most often. It also gives you the measure of the contractor's honesty before money is discussed.

The questions, and the question behind each

The safety lead says: "The harness worked. No injury." The question behind it is: "Can we move on?" Do not. Ask: "Who removed the rail, who was meant to replace it, and what in the job hazard analysis covered deliveries at slab edges?" Then stay silent. The silence after a precise question is where the real answer arrives.

The contractor's project manager says: "We'll recover the slip by month 14." The question behind it is: "Please don't ask how." Ask: "Show me the recovery logic: which activities, which crews, what float you are spending, and what it costs." If the answer is "more labour", ask who pays and whether productivity holds when the crew grows.

The monitor says: "Contingency at 60 percent with the riskiest work ahead concerns us." The question behind it is: "Do you know, or are we discovering this?" Say: "It concerns me too. Here is my estimate at completion range, 21.5 to 22.3 million against 20 million, and the bottom-up reforecast at 21.9. I will put the equity commitment for the gap in writing before the next draw."

Say that out loud now.

Safety first, then the decision, the money and the date; every item leaves with a name beside it.

Lines never to say

Never say "the harness worked, so the system worked". A system that relies on the last line of defence has already failed twice. Never say "we'll make it up later" without the logic. Never say "the contractor says" to a lender as if it were your view; say what you checked. Never promise recovery dates in the room before the schedule analysis exists; say "I will confirm by Friday", and do.

Holding your state

When three bad facts arrive together, slow down. Speak more slowly than you feel like speaking. Write each item on the board with an owner and a date before moving on. If someone becomes defensive, restate the fact without the blame: "The rail was off for two hours. Let's fix the process." Your job is to lower the temperature and raise the precision. If you need a reset, between sessions and parked, not while driving, a few slow breaths with a longer exhale is a practitioner habit many find useful; check that with your doctor if you have any health condition.

The close

A worked close: "Decisions. One: the delivery procedure at slab edges is rewritten by Thursday, the safety lead owns it, and I will walk the site with him Friday. Two: the core-wall recovery logic comes to me by Wednesday; no added labour is approved until I see it. Three: the two allowances are repriced against quotes by next Tuesday, cost consultant owns it. Four: I will send the lender the reforecast and the equity letter before the draw. Anything not on this list did not get decided today." Then stop talking.

A second example of a closing line when the room resists: "If we cannot decide the recovery today, the decision is that nothing changes until Wednesday, and I will not accept a schedule claim for those two days." Silence is also a decision; name it.

After the meeting: the monitor's private question

As people pack up, the monitor stays behind and says quietly: "Off the record, do you trust this contractor?" The question behind it is: "Should I be worried about a failure, not just an overrun?" This is the moment to stay calm and stay factual. Say: "I trust the numbers I have checked. Their safety process failed on Tuesday and their recovery logic is unproven. I will know more on Wednesday, and you will hear it from me before the draw." Never say anything about the contractor's finances or character that you cannot support with a document. Off the record rarely stays off the record, and a careless remark about solvency can do real damage to a business and to you.

When to stay silent

There are three silences in a good review. The first comes after a precise question; wait for the answer rather than filling the gap with a softer version of your question. The second comes after you state a decision; do not explain it three times. The third is the silence you keep when someone blames another person in the room; let them finish, then return to the process: "What changes so it does not happen again?" A worked example: when the contractor's project manager says the guardrail was "the steel erector's problem", you say nothing for a few seconds, then ask the safety lead which job hazard analysis covered the delivery. The facts, not the argument, decide who owns the fix.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a review that reports rather than decides, and treats near misses as good news. The control is an agenda that begins with safety, ends with a written decision list, and carries every open item forward with a name and a date.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner leads with the money because the lender is in the room, and lets safety become an item under "any other business". The lender is watching which one you put first.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught acknowledge, bridge, answer for hostile questions, and "I'll confirm by Friday". You used both today: you acknowledged the monitor's concern, bridged to your range and answered with a commitment you can keep.

Recap

Open with safety, name the decisions you need, ask the precise question behind each soft answer, and stay silent after it. Never rely on the last line of defence or the contractor's word to a lender. Close with a written list of decisions, owners and dates.

Next: Kema, on the Checkpoint: a mock interview, a recorded three-minute explanation and the rules you have committed to so far.
checklist: Safety is always the first agenda item.
I ask who, what changed and how we know it is fixed after any near miss.
I ask for recovery logic before accepting any recovery date.
I give the lender my own estimate at completion range and reforecast.
I never present the contractor's view as my own.
Every agenda item leaves with an owner and a date.
I close by reading the decision list aloud and then stop talking.
head: Field checklist
speak: The monthly review is where the owner's control system works or performs. I open with safety, every time: after a near miss I ask who removed the protection, who was meant to replace it, and how we know it is fixed across the site, then I stay silent. A harness that arrests a fall means two layers already failed. Then I name the decisions I need. When the contractor promises recovery, I ask for the logic: activities, crews, float and cost. When the lender's monitor is concerned, I agree, give my estimate at completion range and my bottom-up reforecast, and commit to put any equity in writing before the draw. I never pass on the contractor's word as my own view, and I never promise dates I have not analysed. I slow down when bad news stacks up. I close with a written list of decisions, owners and dates, read it aloud, and stop talking.
terms: Near miss — an incident that could have caused injury or damage but did not, treated as evidence that a control failed.
Recovery logic — the specific activities, crews, float and costs a contractor proposes to regain lost time.
Decision list — the written record at the end of a meeting of each decision, its owner and its date.

hostile.q: Your contingency is 60 percent spent at 45 percent complete. Why shouldn't I stop funding until you prove this project is under control?
hostile.a: Because I can show you control now. My estimate at completion range is 21.5 to 22.3 million against 20 million, and my bottom-up reforecast is 21.9. I will commit the equity for that gap in writing before the draw. The two allowances driving it are being repriced against quotes by Tuesday, and no recovery labour is approved until I have tested the logic. You will have all of it in writing before the draw request arrives.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Checkpoint: The Owner's Control System
summary: This checkpoint tests the owner's control phase out loud: six mock interview questions, a three-minute recorded explanation scored on four measures, and a read-through of every rule you have committed to. Progress is measured by what you can say under pressure, not by what you recognise on a page.
body:
You have finished the owner's control phase. Today you find out whether you can explain it under pressure, without notes, and you write down a score you can beat at the next checkpoint.

Recall

Q. What is the first item on a monthly project review agenda, and why?

A. Safety, because it tells the room a guardrail outranks a schedule and because a near miss is evidence that a control failed.

Q. What is the Last Planner System?

A. A collaborative planning method in which the people who do the work make reliable short-term commitments and track the percentage of commitments kept each week.

Q. What is a promote in an equity waterfall?

A. The sponsor's share of profit above its share of capital, paid once investors clear agreed return hurdles. The splits are commercial practice.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, reading builds recognition, and recognition feels like knowledge until a lender asks you a hard question. A checkpoint moves the phase from recognition to recall, and from recall to performance. The score you write today is the baseline for the next checkpoint.

The mock interview

Answer each question aloud before reading the model answer. Be strict.

Question 1. What does "the owner is in control" mean?

Answer: Four things at once: I decided in advance what good looks like, in a charter and a frozen baseline; I measure against it monthly with my own numbers; someone with the right authority decides what to do about each gap; and every decision is recorded. Missing any one, I am a spectator.

Question 2. CPI is 0.90 and SPI is 0.90 on a 20 million dollar budget. What is the estimate at completion?

Answer: The optimistic alarm is budget over CPI, about 22.2 million. The pessimistic one is spend to date plus remaining budget over CPI times SPI; at 8 million spent and 7.2 million earned, that is 8 plus 12.8 over 0.81, about 23.8 million. I follow the alarm with a bottom-up reforecast.

Question 3. Your contract has a GMP. Is your cost fixed?

Answer: No. A GMP caps the contractor's cost for a defined scope. Owner changes, overrunning allowances, escalation outside agreed bands, exclusions and owner-allocated risks sit outside it. The qualifications list is the real price.

Question 4. Who can be cited for a fall hazard on an American multi-employer site?

Answer: Under OSHA's multi-employer policy, potentially the employer that created the hazard, the one whose workers were exposed, the one responsible for correcting it, and the one controlling the site. I manage safety through the contract rather than by directing trades. Verify the current policy against the primary source.

Question 5. How do you explain an overrun?

Answer: Start from the final account, take off contingency, and split the rest into owner changes, allowances and escalation, scope gaps, and delay and productivity, then add interest and soft costs. Beside each cause I name the control that should have caught it.

Question 6. What did Sampoong teach you?

Answer: Rule 54: no change to structure, use or load goes ahead without the engineer of record's written approval in the change log, and a structural warning means evacuate first and meet second. When every incentive points one way, the control must point the other.

Say that out loud now.

The recorded explanation

Now the real test. Take out your phone, open the voice recorder, and record a three-minute explanation of this phase as if to a new equity partner who has never built anything. Use this structure: the control loop, plan, measure, decide, record; earned value and the estimate at completion; what a GMP and a notice clause really do; and one failure case with its prevention rule. No notes. Do not restart if you stumble; stumbling is data.

Listen back once and score yourself from 1 to 5 on each of four measures:

  1. Accuracy. Were the definitions and the arithmetic right? A 5 has no errors; a 3 has one material slip.
  2. Structure. Did you lead with the bottom line and follow the four-part order? A 5 could be written down as an outline.
  3. Composure. Was the pace steady, with pauses instead of filler? A 5 sounds like someone who has chaired this meeting many times.
  4. The hard question. Did you raise the biggest risk unprompted, such as a baseline that quietly moves or an approval outside the matrix? A 5 names the weakness before the listener can.

A worked example of honest scoring. If you said "CPI is actual cost over earned value", you inverted it, and accuracy is a 2 whatever else you said, because a lender would catch it in a sentence. If you spent forty seconds on what a project manager is before reaching the loop, structure is a 3.

A second example. If your explanation was accurate and well ordered but never mentioned what you would do when the indices fell below one, the hard question is a 3. Knowing the measure without the response is half the skill.

What to do with the scores

Take your lowest score and act on that one alone this week. Accuracy: rebuild the definition in your own words and test it against Day 3. Structure: write the four parts on a card and record again using only the card. Composure: record at a deliberately slower pace and count filler words on playback. The hard question: open the next recording with "The thing that breaks owner control is...". Record again at the end of the week. A move from 3 to 4 on one measure is real progress.

Rules I will not break

Below this lesson is the list of rules you have committed to so far, one from each failure case. Read each rule below aloud, then restate it in your own words. Mark any rule you cannot restate without looking, and reread the lesson it came from this week.

A model outline for the three minutes

Compare your recording with this outline only after you have scored it. Opening, about twenty seconds: "Owner control is one loop. I plan, I measure against the plan, I decide what to do about each gap, and I record the decision. If one part is missing, I am not in control." The loop, about forty seconds: the charter and the approval matrix, the frozen baseline, the work breakdown tying each element to one cost code and one schedule activity, and the monthly decision meeting. The numbers, about forty seconds: earned value, the two indices, the two alarms for the estimate at completion, and the efficiency the rest of the job would need to finish on budget.

The paper, about forty seconds: authority comes from the contract and from conduct, notice clauses can end a right, a guaranteed maximum price caps a scope and not the project, and shared safety duties follow control. The failure case, about thirty seconds: Sampoong, and Rule 54. Close, about ten seconds: "The thing that breaks owner control is a baseline that quietly moves, so I keep the original frozen and explain every difference with a logged change." If your three minutes ran out before the failure case, you spent too long on definitions. If you finished in two, you skipped the reasons. Either way, the outline tells you which part to rebuild.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk at a checkpoint is grading what you meant rather than what you said. The recording does not care what you meant. Score the tape.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the model answers instead of saying them first, and feels prepared. Reading gives the feeling of mastery without the evidence.

Callback

At the Week 47 checkpoint you explained the capital stack and the lender's view. Listen to that recording if you kept it, then to today's. The owner's control system is what makes those financing promises true: a lender's covenant is only as safe as the owner's monthly loop.

Recap

Answer the six questions aloud first. Record three minutes without notes, score accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question from 1 to 5, and write the scores and date in your decision journal. Then read every rule aloud and restate it.

Next: Omar, on First Principles: structure as design, the six lenses, the flow of funds and control, and sequencing.

head: Rules I will not break
speak: This checkpoint closes the owner's control phase. The loop is plan, measure, decide, record: a charter and frozen baseline, monthly earned value on my own numbers, change control at the right authority, and a decision log. Cost performance is earned value over actual cost; schedule performance is earned value over planned value. Budget over CPI is the optimistic estimate at completion; remaining budget over CPI times SPI is the pessimistic one. A guaranteed maximum price caps a defined scope, not my project. Notice clauses can extinguish rights, so I keep a notice register. On an American site, safety duties can be shared across employers, so I manage safety through the contract. I explain an overrun by reconciling every dollar to a cause and a control. Rule 54 keeps changes to structure, use and load behind the engineer of record. Today I record three minutes, score four measures, and act on the lowest.
terms: Checkpoint — a scheduled test of a whole phase, done aloud and scored, to move knowledge from recognition to recall.
Accuracy score — a 1 to 5 rating of whether definitions and numbers in a recorded explanation were right.
Hard-question score — a 1 to 5 rating of whether you raised the biggest risk before the listener asked.

hostile.q: You have explained the control loop well. What actually stops you overriding it when you are under pressure?
hostile.a: Three things outside my own willpower. The approval matrix is in the contract and a partner resolution, so an override is visible. The engineer of record must sign any change to structure, use or load, whatever I want. And the decision log records who decided and on what evidence, which my lender and partners read. I built those controls precisely because I will be under pressure, and I will want to skip them.
